title: Chapter 1: Mud, Canals, and the First Ledgers

notes.phrase: less than 100 to 150 millimeters of rain
notes.note: Southern Mesopotamia's arid baseline (<100–150 mm annual rainfall) lies well below the ~200–250 mm threshold needed for reliable rain-fed grain farming.

notes.phrase: April and May, brown floodwater surged
notes.note: Unlike the late-summer Nile inundation, Anatolian snowmelt drives violent April–May surges on the Tigris and Euphrates during winter barley harvest, requiring both protective spring dikes and autumn storage/regulator works.

notes.phrase: natural raised levees, the riverbeds actually sat slightly higher
notes.note: Alluvial silt deposition built raised riverbanks above the surrounding plain, enabling gravity-fed feeder canals while leaving low-lying backslope basins vulnerable to poor drainage.

notes.phrase: one grain of barley returned fifteen to thirty grains
notes.note: On the Sumerian ox-drawn seeder plow (cutting seed waste by roughly half) and irrigated barley return ratios of 1:15 to 1:30 compared with 1:5 to 1:8 on rain-fed land.

Archaeological estimates place Late Uruk (c. 3200–3000 BCE) at roughly 250–400 hectares with an estimated population around 40,000 residents—an archaeological reconstruction rather than an ancient census.

sections.heading: 2. Politics, Work Shifts, and the First Ledgers

notes.phrase: Nobody in early Uruk left a diary
notes.note: Because early Uruk left administrative records rather than narrative political histories, historians reconstruct early city governance by combining archaeology with later third-millennium inscriptions and epics (such as Gilgamesh and Akka, ETCSL 1.8.1.1). On temple legitimacy and evolving kingship (lugal), see Jacobsen (1976), Steinkeller (1999), Liverani (2006), and Van De Mieroop (2016); on city assemblies and emergency leadership, see Jacobsen's classic thesis (1943) and the broader comparative survey in Graeber and Wengrow (2021).

notes.phrase: often fifteen to thirty days each year
notes.note: Mandatory seasonal corvée labor shifts (Sumerian dusu) mobilized free households for canal dredging, dike repair, harvesting, and brickmaking; wealthier citizens could later commute shifts with silver or hired substitutes.

notes.phrase: mold-made clay vessels called beveled-rim bowls
notes.note: Hans Nissen (1970, p. 137) proposed that mass-produced Uruk beveled-rim bowls (~0.8–1 liter) served as standardized grain or porridge ration vessels. Daniel T. Potts (2009, pp. 1–23) reviews the debate and argues instead that they functioned primarily as clay baking molds for standardized bread loaves (which institutional bakeries could also issue to workers).
On the transition from clay tokens sealed inside cylinder-sealed hollow clay envelopes (bullae) to impressed proto-cuneiform tablets (c. 3500–3100 BCE).
Approximately 85–90% of the ~5,000 archaic Uruk tablets are economic and administrative records, while 10–15% are standardized lexical word-lists copied by apprentice scribes.

notes.phrase: 29,086 measures of barley received over 37 months, signed Kushim.
notes.note: Primary artifact: Uruk III proto-cuneiform barley-accounting tablet cataloged as MSVO 3, 29 (formerly Schøyen Collection MS 1717; c. 3100 BCE). The quoted line is a standard modern summary of the tablet's accounting signs (29,086 measures of barley, 37 months, KU.ŠIM), not a continuous prose sentence in the original clay. Scholars note that 'Kushim' may denote either an individual administrator's name or an institutional office title.

Ur III administrative archives (c. 2100–2000 BCE) document standardized monthly barley rations (še-ba) of 60 sila (~60 liters) for adult male workers, 30–40 sila for adult women, and 10–20 sila for children, supplemented with annual wool allowances (4 minas / ~2 kg), oil, and beer.

sections.heading: 3. Mudbrick Mountains, Wool Workshops, and Sealed Promises

notes.phrase: Southern Mesopotamia had almost no building stone
notes.note: Alluvial southern Mesopotamia lacked local stone quarries, metal ores, and long-span structural timber (date-palm wood is fibrous), relying on mud, marsh reeds, bitumen seepage, barley, and sheep's wool.

notes.phrase: roughly 64 meters long by 45 meters wide
notes.note: Monumental mudbrick construction of the White Temple on the Anu Ziggurat (Uruk) and King Ur-Nammu's Ziggurat of Ur (c. 2100 BCE): ~64 × 45 m footprint, sun-dried mudbrick core reinforced with woven reed mats and cables, ~2.4 m kiln-baked brick outer casing set in bitumen mortar, and rainwater weep-holes.

notes.phrase: cedar timber from the mountains of Lebanon
notes.note: Long-distance trade imported cedar from Lebanon and the Amanus range, copper from Oman (Magan), and lapis lazuli from Afghanistan, financed heavily by woven wool textiles produced in large workshops employing hundreds of women.

notes.phrase: wrapped the whole tablet inside a thin outer coat of wet clay
notes.note: Ur III and Old Babylonian legal practice (c. 2100–1700 BCE) enclosed dried contract tablets inside summary-inscribed, cylinder-sealed clay envelopes that courts could crack open to settle disputes.

sections.heading: 4. The Salt Trap and the Next River

notes.note: In poorly drained basins behind raised river levees, evaporation under >45°C (113°F) summer heat drew saline groundwater upward and concentrated mineral salts in the root zone.

notes.phrase: wheat still made up about 16 percent
notes.note: In their landmark 1958 Science study of southern temple harvest records between c. 2400 BCE and 1700 BCE, Thorkild Jacobsen and Robert McC. Adams tracked salt-sensitive wheat falling from roughly 16% of recorded southern grain harvests to under 2% (and vanishing altogether in some southern cities), eroding southern surplus capacity as political weight shifted north toward Babylon.
